questions.stem: B cell mediated hypersensitivity reaction is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Arthus phenomenon

 

Hypersensitivity reactions involving B cells are those that involve antibody production, because B cells differentiate into plasma cells which secrete antibodies.

 

Hypersensitivity Types Involving B Cells:

  • Type I – IgE (e.g., anaphylaxis)
  • Type II – IgG/IgM (e.g., hemolytic anemia)
  • Type III – Immune complex (e.g., Arthus reaction)
     

Arthus Phenomenon (Type III):
 

A localized immune complex-mediated hypersensitivity reaction
 

Caused by IgG antibodies binding to antigen → complement activation → inflammation
 

Classic example of B cell–mediated (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity
    
Other options: 
 

Option B. Contact dermatitis – Type IV (T-cell mediated)
 

Option C. Delayed-type hypersensitivity – Type IV (T-cell mediated)
 

Option D. Tuberculin reaction – Also Type IV (T-cell mediated)

 

Educational Objective:- 

 

Arthus phenomenon is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction mediated by B cells through IgG antibody-antigen immune complexes causing localized inflammation, while contact dermatitis, DTH, and tuberculin reactions are all Type IV T-cell mediated reactions. Remember: "B cells = Antibodies = Types I, II, III" vs "T cells = Type IV

questions.stem: Lens Protein Is an Example Of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Sequestered antigen

 

Lens protein in the eye is normally hidden from the immune system during development because of the blood-ocular barrier. This makes it a classic example of a sequestered antigen.
 

It is an antigen isolated from the immune system in immunologically privileged sites like:
 

  • Eye (e.g., lens proteins)
  • Brain
  • Testes
     

If trauma or inflammation exposes these antigens to the immune system later in life, the body may recognize them as foreign, leading to an autoimmune response.
 

Other options:

 

Option A. Cross-reacting foreign antigen – Seen in molecular mimicry, not lens protein
 

Option C. Molecular mimicry – Refers to foreign antigens resembling self-antigens (e.g., rheumatic fever)
 

Option D. Forbidden clone – Refers to autoreactive lymphocytes that escape deletion during development

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lens proteins are sequestered antigens - normally hidden from the immune system by the blood-ocular barrier during development, so if exposed later through trauma or surgery, they're recognized as foreign and can trigger autoimmune uveitis (sympathetic ophthalmia). Remember: "Sequestered = Hidden in privileged sites (eye, brain, testes)."

questions.stem: Best example of syngeneic graft:

options.label: C
options.text: Between two members of same or different species

options.label: D
options.text: Between two sites of same person

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Between monozygotic twins

 

A syngeneic graft (also called isograft) is a type of transplant between two genetically identical individuals. They are genetically identical, so grafts between them are syngeneic.
 

Other options: 
 

Option A. Between dizygotic twins: They are like regular siblings — not genetically identical, so not syngeneic.

 

Option C. Between two members of same or different species: Could refer to allograft (same species) or xenograft (different species) — not syngeneic.

 

Option D. Between two sites of same person: This is an autograft, not syngeneic.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Syngeneic grafts (isografts) occur between genetically identical individuals, with monozygotic twins being the best example as they share 100% identical DNA, ensuring no immune rejection. Remember: "SYN = SAME genetics" - monozygotic twins are the only naturally occurring genetically identical humans.

questions.stem: Graft versus Host reactions occurs only if:

options.label: C
options.text: Recipient must not reject the graft

options.label: D
options.text: Recipient is not on immunosuppressive drugs

questions.answerText: Recipient must not reject the graft
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Recipient must not reject the graft

 

Immunocompetent T cells in the donor graft recognize the recipient’s tissues as foreign and attack them. It is common after bone marrow (hematopoietic stem cell) transplantation.
 

GVHD requires three essential conditions:

  1. The graft must contain immunocompetent T cells
  2. The recipient must be immunocompromised (cannot reject the graft) 
  3. There must be HLA mismatch between graft and host
     

Other options: 
 

Option A: Graft contains immunocompetent B cells – this is false, Graft should contain immunocompetent T cells not B cells to cause GVHD
 

Option B: Graft contains macrophages – THIS IS FALSE,  Macrophages are not primary effectors in GVHD

 

Option D: Recipient is not on immunosuppressive drugs – While immunosuppression increases GVHD risk, it’s not the defining factor .

 

Educational Objective: 

 

GVHD occurs when immunocompetent T cells from the donor graft attack the immunocompromised recipient's tissues - requiring three conditions: graft contains T cells, recipient cannot reject the graft (immunocompromised), and HLA mismatch exists. Remember: "GVHD = Graft T cells attack defenseless host
